title: AIP Morning Brief — 27 Nov — When the grid build-out becomes the risk
show_notes:
# AIP Morning Brief — Friday 27 November 2026

Guests: Priya (regulation specialist), Sofia (enterprise software and AI analyst)

**Top line:** Britain's grid operator issued its third electricity margin warning of the week on Thursday, and blamed it partly on network constraints created by the transmission owners' own maintenance and reinforcement work. In the US, a Thanksgiving storm cut power to more than 900,000 customers and forced a water utility serving 1.9 million people into an essential-use-only request, its second power-driven crisis in two months. On both sides of the Atlantic, the build-out itself is now a reliability risk, and that makes sequencing and prioritising capital work a board-level issue for utilities.

*A quieter 36 hours for competitor and IFS news (US Thanksgiving), so today goes deeper on the infrastructure stories.*

## Stories

**1. UK grid: third margin warning in a week, and the upgrade programme is part of the problem** · HIGH (R4 S4 T5 I3 = 4.0) · Metrics: pipeline timing, win rate, deal size
On Thursday 26 Nov the National Energy System Operator (NESO) issued electricity margin notices (EMNs) for 8am–noon and noon–8pm, its third alert this week. Aggregator reports put the afternoon shortfall at more than 2.7GW (single-sourced, treat as approximate), with wind about 2.5GW below forecast and cold weather lifting demand. NESO called the notice "routine and precautionary" with no risk to supplies. It blamed "significant constraints on the network caused by maintenance and reinforcement work by transmission owners", which cut north–south transfer capacity, so Scottish wind was paid to switch off and replaced further south. A tracker put Thursday's balancing actions above £6m, and the Telegraph reports wasted-wind costs above £2bn so far in 2026. Background: the National Audit Office (NAO) warned in September that constraint costs, £1.9bn in 2025-26, could reach £7.8bn by 2030 without faster delivery. Of 80 projects NESO called necessary for Clean Power 2030, 64 are under way, mostly at an early stage. On-time connection offers fell from 64% (2019-20) to 16% (2023-24).

*Why it matters (opinion):* this is a new argument for portfolio planning. Building the grid takes circuits out of service, and those outages are now visibly costing consumers money in a week when the price cap rose 26%. Expect Ofgem and NESO to push transmission and distribution owners on outage coordination, delivery assurance and evidence that work is sequenced to minimise system cost. That turns asset investment planning (AIP) from "which projects" into "which projects, in what order, with what outage windows". Winners: owners who can show optimised plans. Losers: anyone whose ED3 business plan (due December) can't show it.
- **Base:** strengthens the delivery-assurance case in UK TO/DNO conversations; no immediate change to pipeline timing.
- **Best:** Ofgem formalises outage-optimisation and delivery reporting in RIIO-3 reopeners or ED3 guidance, pulling UK portfolio-planning demand forward by a few quarters (illustrative).
- **Worst:** affordability politics turn into blanket scrutiny that slows approvals and procurement, lengthening UK sales cycles.
**What to watch:** more EMNs in December and January, the tightest months in NESO's Winter Outlook; ED3 business plans in December; any Ofgem or NESO response on outage planning.
Sources: [Telegraph via Yahoo](https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/grid-operator-issues-third-warning-114146002.html) · [IndexBox](https://www.indexbox.io/blog/uk-power-system-margin-tightens-as-cold-snap-persists/) · [NAO](https://nao.org.uk/press-releases/delays-to-electricity-grid-upgrades-risk-higher-bills/)

**2. US Thanksgiving storm: 900,000+ outages, and a water utility's power problem strikes twice** · HIGH (R4 S3 T5 I3 = 3.75) · Metrics: pipeline timing, win rate, churn risk (low)
On 26 Nov a coastal storm left more than 900,000 customers without power by evening (PowerOutage.us): Pennsylvania over 200,000, Maryland over 172,000, Virginia over 150,000, Missouri over 100,000. Gusts reached 74mph in West Virginia and New Jersey declared a statewide emergency. At 2:30pm WSSC Water asked all 1.9 million customers in Montgomery and Prince George's counties to use water for essentials only, citing intermittent power disruptions. Its Potomac plant had power but unstable production. The Patuxent plant was out for planned maintenance and also hit by storm power problems. The water stayed safe, with no boil notice. Background: the Potomac plant, which supplies about 75% of WSSC's water, lost power on 29 Sep and triggered the same request. WSSC's CEO told the county council the plant's power systems are aged and fragile, with too little redundancy. An assessment found 10 electrical projects costing about $155M, three of them priority projects worth about $130M. Only $4.5M is budgeted this year, with $6M proposed for FY2028. The base rate proposal is 7%, against 11.7% recommended in a draft cost-of-service study.

*Why it matters (opinion):* two lessons. First, interdependency: water risk is often power risk, which cross-asset risk models should capture. Second, maintenance timing: a planned outage at one plant coincided with a storm at the other. Councils and regulators will now ask utilities to show their resilience investment is ranked by risk and fits what customers can afford. That is the AIP pitch in one sentence. Second-order: expect US storm-cost recovery filings and more state commission scrutiny of resilience plans in early 2027.
- **Base:** resilience and redundancy climb US water and power capex priorities over 12–24 months; supportive, but no near-term pipeline change.
- **Best:** post-event reviews explicitly demand risk-quantified, cross-asset prioritisation, improving win rates where that is the evaluation criterion (illustrative).
- **Worst:** storm-recovery costs and affordability fights (7% vs 11.7%) squeeze discretionary software budgets and push deals right.
**What to watch:** WSSC's FY2028 budget and rate decision; utility storm-cost filings; any Maryland review of the repeat outage.
Sources: [National Pulse](https://thenationalpulse.com/2026/11/26/powerful-thanksgiving-storm-unleashes-floods-leaves-900000-without-power/) · [GSM Global – WSSC](https://gsmglobalnews.com/article/d20261126-gap1435-wsscwater1.html) · [WJLA – $155M upgrades](https://wjla.com/news/local/wssc-water-potomac-filtration-plant-outage-bills-rate-increase-montgomery-county-prince-georges-maryland-electrical-upgrades-155-million-customer-affordability) · [Fox 5 DC](https://www.fox5dc.com/news/wssc-water-plant-outage-under-review-montgomery-county-council) · [WaterWorld](https://www.waterworld.com/water-utility-management/news/55409037/wssc-water-asks-19-million-customers-to-conserve-amid-plant-power-issue)

**3. Thames Water back in court today to push 2027 debt to 2028** · HIGH (R5 S3 T4 I3 = 3.75) · Metrics: pipeline timing (UK water), churn risk (sector)
The High Court convening hearing is today (27 Nov) for two linked Part 26A restructuring plans. They would extend all senior secured debt due in 2027 (super senior, Class A and B) to March 2028, and stretch the "stable platform period" that expires 22 March 2027. Creditors holding more than £12bn have signed up. Timetable: accession deadline 11 Dec, creditor meetings 17 Dec, sanction hearing 13 Jan 2027, effective around the week of 1 Feb 2027. Separately, creditors approved a £2.4bn super senior upsize, with a first tranche of up to £600m, extending liquidity into autumn 2027 (9fin). Thames says the extension supports its "record AMP8 capital investment programme". The board, Ofwat and other regulators have made no decision on the London & Valley Water (L&VW) creditor recapitalisation, and 9fin reports a revised deal could reach Ofwat as early as December.

*Why it matters (opinion):* this buys time, not a fix. It keeps AMP8 delivery going, but a company in a court-supervised holding pattern is not one that makes bold new commitments. The sector-wide effect matters more: every month Thames stays unresolved keeps UK water financing costs and investor caution higher.
- **Base:** extension sanctioned in January; AMP8 continues cautiously; non-essential procurement stays slow until recapitalisation.
- **Best:** a recapitalisation agreed in 2027 brings equity and a reset business plan that needs rigorous investment prioritisation.
- **Worst:** talks fail and special administration follows, freezing discretionary spend and lifting sector financing costs.
**What to watch:** today's hearing outcome; 17 Dec creditor vote; any revised L&VW proposal to Ofwat.
Sources: [Thames Water announcement](https://www.thameswater.co.uk/news/2026/nov/rp15-tsa-and-psl-announcement) · [9fin](https://www.9fin.com/insights/thames-water-extend-2027-debt-recap)

**4. Octave (ex-Hexagon EAM) six months on: growth guide cut, Russell entry next** · MEDIUM (R3 S3 T3 I3 = 3.0) · Metrics: win rate, pricing power
Octave Intelligence, spun out of Hexagon in May 2026 and listed in New York (OCTV) and Stockholm, owns Octave Attune EAM (formerly HxGN EAM / Infor EAM). An analysis of its filings published 24 Nov (Every Spin-Off newsletter, secondary) says 2026 organic growth guidance was cut to 0.5–2% from 3–4%. It puts ARR at about $1.17bn in September (guidance $1.185–1.205bn) and gross revenue retention at about 97%. It also reports a $625m payment to Hexagon at separation funded partly by about $524m of term loans, and material weaknesses in internal controls. FTSE Russell's preliminary list adds Octave to the Russell indices after the close on 11 Dec. On AI, IDC rates Attune a Leader in AI-enabled EAM; its generative assistant Aria launched in late 2024 and agentic features are promised for 2026.

*Why it matters (opinion, medium confidence):* a big EAM incumbent with sticky customers (97% GRR) but little growth, new debt and controls remediation is a distracted competitor. That can help in head-to-head evaluations. But under pressure to show growth, it could also discount or bundle planning into EAM renewals.
- **Base:** strong installed base, limited appetite for aggressive pricing or big R&D bets; little near-term change.
- **Best:** distraction opens win-rate opportunities where AIP and EAM are evaluated together (illustrative).
- **Worst:** Octave bundles or discounts investment-planning features into EAM deals, pressuring price.
**What to watch:** Russell inclusion 11 Dec; Q4 results early 2027; agentic AI release.
Sources: [Hexagon IR – Octave separation](https://investors.hexagon.com/share-information/octave-separation) · [Every Spin-Off #11](https://everyspinofff.substack.com/p/every-spin-off-11-octave-intelligence) · [Octave – IDC MarketScape](https://www.octave.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/octave-named-leader-in-idc-marketscape)

**5. Bank of England flags AI-linked fragility; software multiples keep paying for growth** · HIGH (R4 S4 T3 I3 = 3.5) · Metrics: cost of capital, valuation, pricing power
The Financial Stability Report (26 Nov) kept the countercyclical buffer at 2%. It warned that AI-related interconnections raise the risk of several vulnerabilities crystallising at once. It notes hyperscaler bond issuance set to exceed $305bn in 2026 (about 8% of global investment-grade issuance), and says AI-linked equities fell sharply after the US midterms while valuations remain "stretched on some measures". The UK 10-year gilt yield is up about 40bp since July, mainly on expected policy rates. Meritech's latest pulse (25 Nov): median software ARR multiple 4.3x (from 4.5x), median net dollar retention stable at 107–109%, and companies growing faster at a similar Rule of 40 trade at 7.3x versus 4.1x.

*Why it matters (opinion):* higher discount rates plus AI nervousness keep multiples compressed. What still gets paid for is growth and retention. For PE-owned software, that means owners will want growth that pays back quickly and NRR above the public median.
- **Base:** multiples stay compressed into 2027; growth and NRR remain the valuation levers.
- **Best:** AI volatility rotates investors toward mission-critical vertical software with durable retention.
- **Worst:** an AI-credit wobble tightens financing, pushing owners to favour cash over growth investment.
**What to watch:** Fed (9 Dec) and ECB (17 Dec) decisions; next Meritech pulse.
Sources: [BoE FSR Nov 2026](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/financial-stability-report/2026/november-2026) · [Meritech Software Pulse](https://meritech.substack.com/p/meritech-software-pulse-23-november) · [Multiples.vc](https://multiples.vc/insights/software-saas-valuation-multiples)

## Macro & SaaS pulse
- **Fed:** markets price about a 96% chance of a 25bp hike at the December meeting after a hotter-than-expected October core PCE print ([Investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/forex-news/asia-fx-won-muted-after-bok-hikes-rates-dollar-steady-5052015), [FinScans](https://finscans.com/news/2026/11/26/usd-gains-face-resistance-as-markets-price-96-chance-of)).
- **FX:** the dollar index sits just below its 2026 highs; GBP/USD about 1.31, EUR/USD about 1.096, AUD/USD about 0.665, USD/JPY near 159 ([Investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/forex-news/asia-fx-won-muted-after-bok-hikes-rates-dollar-steady-5052015)).
- **Europe:** euro-area inflation is at 4.0%, double the ECB target, with a December hike widely expected ([Eurostat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-euro-indicators/w/2-18112026-ap)).
- **Energy:** Brent about $92 a barrel versus $75 in July, per the BoE ([FSR](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/financial-stability-report/2026/november-2026)).
- **SaaS:** vertical SaaS trades at a median 2.0x EV/NTM revenue, horizontal at 1.9x ([Multiples.vc](https://multiples.vc/insights/software-saas-valuation-multiples)).

## 3 things to raise with the CFO
1. **The "build-out risk" narrative is now public. Use it.** UK constraint costs (£1.9bn last year, potentially £7.8bn by 2030) and this week's margin warnings tie grid reliability to how well capital work is sequenced. *Ask:* agree that UK pipeline reviews tag opportunities where outage and delivery optimisation is a buying driver, and fund some targeted marketing around ED3 plans in December.
2. **Resilience spend is rising, and so is affordability pressure.** WSSC's $155M electrical need against a 7% vs 11.7% rate debate is the US pattern in miniature. *Ask:* model a scenario where US water and municipal deals slip one to two quarters on budget squeeze, against an upside where resilience mandates speed them up; check the forecast isn't assuming only the upside.
3. **Benchmark the board story against what markets pay for.** Public software is paid for growth and NRR (median NDR 107–109%), not margin alone, and a large EAM rival is guiding to roughly flat growth. *Ask:* frame the next board pack's ARR bridge around NRR versus public medians, and confirm deal desk guardrails if competitors start bundling planning features into EAM renewals.

dialogue.text: Morning, and welcome to the AIP Morning Brief for Friday the twenty-seventh of November. I'm Maya.

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: So the theme today is that building the network is now a reliability risk in its own right. Which makes the order you do the work in a very big deal.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: Let's start in Britain. Yesterday the National Energy System Operator, known as NESO, issued what's called an electricity margin notice. dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: And NESO was quick to say it's routine and precautionary, with no risk to supplies and nothing customers need to do. That's fair.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: And the less obvious stuff?

dialogue.speaker: GUEST_REG
dialogue.text: NESO pointed to significant constraints on the network caused by maintenance and reinforcement work by the transmission owners. NESO pays it to switch off and buys replacement power, mostly gas, further south.

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: Which is the irony. The work that's meant to fix the bottleneck is making the bottleneck worse while it happens.

dialogue.speaker: GUEST_REG
dialogue.text: Exactly, and it isn't cheap. One tracker put Thursday's balancing actions at more than six million pounds. The Telegraph reports the cost of wasted wind has passed two billion pounds so far this year.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR

dialogue.speaker: GUEST_REG

Of the eighty projects NESO said were needed for the Clean Power twenty thirty target, sixty-four are under way, but most are at an early stage.

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: Here's why that matters. Until now the grid investment story in Britain has mostly been about how much and which projects. This week shows a third question, which is in what order, and with what outage windows. Every circuit you take out for reinforcement has a system cost, and in a cold, still week that cost turns up on the balancing bill.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: So who pushes on that?

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: Ofgem and NESO, I'd expect. This lands in the same week the price cap went up twenty-six percent. The affordability politics are brutal right now. So I'd expect much more pressure on the transmission and distribution companies to show they're coordinating outages and sequencing work to keep system costs down. That's squarely an asset investment planning problem.

dialogue.speaker: GUEST_REG
dialogue.text: I'd add a note of caution, Jordan. Outage planning sits partly with NESO's own operational teams and partly with the transmission owners' delivery teams. dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST

Watch today's hearing and the creditor vote on the seventeenth of December.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: Now to competitors. Octave is the business Hexagon spun out in May, and it owns the enterprise asset management product many listeners will know as Infor EAM, now called Octave Attune. Joining us to talk about it is Sofia, our enterprise software and AI analyst. Morning, Sofia.

dialogue.speaker: GUEST_TECH
dialogue.text: Morning, Maya. Morning, Jordan.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: Why are we talking about Octave today?

dialogue.speaker: GUEST_TECH
dialogue.text: Two reasons. First, a detailed analysis of its filings came out this week from a newsletter that tracks spin-offs. That's a secondary source, so treat the figures with some care. Second, it's about to join the Russell indices after the market closes on the eleventh of December, which brings a new set of investors.

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: So what does the analysis say?

dialogue.speaker: GUEST_TECH
dialogue.text: The headline is growth. According to that analysis, Octave cut its twenty twenty-six organic growth guidance to between half a percent and two percent, down from three to four percent back in March. Annual recurring revenue was about one point one seven billion dollars in September, against guidance of roughly one point one nine to one point two billion for the year. And gross revenue retention is about ninety-seven percent, which is very sticky.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: So a big, loyal customer base that isn't growing much.

dialogue.speaker: GUEST_TECH
dialogue.text: Pretty much. And there are a couple of extra weights. At separation Octave paid Hexagon six hundred and twenty-five million dollars, partly funded with roughly five hundred and twenty-four million of term loans. The analysis also reports that Octave disclosed material weaknesses in its internal controls, which it'll be spending time and money fixing.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: What about the product? Everyone's talking about AI.

dialogue.speaker: GUEST_TECH
dialogue.text: IDC rates Attune a leader in AI-enabled enterprise asset management, which is a real endorsement. Its generative AI assistant, called Aria, first shipped in late twenty twenty-four, and agentic features, meaning AI that takes multi-step actions, are promised for twenty twenty-six. So the product is credible. What's in question is how much the company can invest behind it.

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: Here's my take, medium confidence because of the source. A large incumbent with ninety-seven percent retention, almost no growth, new debt and a controls clean-up is a distracted competitor. That tends to show up as slower roadmaps and less flexible deal teams.

dialogue.speaker: GUEST_TECH
dialogue.text: I'd disagree a little, Jordan. A low-growth incumbent under public-market pressure often does the opposite. It gets aggressive. The easiest growth lever is selling more to the installed base, and one way to do that is to bundle planning or investment features into renewals at a token price.

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: That's fair, and it's my worst case. So, base case, Octave stays a strong incumbent with little appetite for big pricing moves or R&D bets, and not much changes near term. Best case, its distraction opens up win-rate opportunities where asset investment planning and asset management are evaluated together. That's illustrative. Worst case, it bundles or discounts planning features into its asset management deals and that pressures price.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: Sofia, what are you watching?

dialogue.speaker: GUEST_TECH
dialogue.text: The Russell inclusion on the eleventh of December, its fourth-quarter results early next year, and whether the agentic AI features actually ship. If they slip, that tells you where the money's going.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: Sofia, thank you.

dialogue.speaker: GUEST_TECH
dialogue.text: Thanks for having me.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: Last story. The Bank of England published its Financial Stability Report yesterday. It kept the countercyclical capital buffer at its neutral two percent, but the tone on AI was notably more cautious.

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: The Bank said AI-related links across the system raise the chance that several vulnerabilities crystallise at once. It noted that bond issuance by the big cloud companies is set to top three hundred and five billion dollars this year, about eight percent of global investment-grade issuance. And it said AI-linked shares fell sharply after the US midterms, while valuations still look stretched on some measures.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: And rates?

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: The UK ten-year gilt yield is up about forty basis points since July, mainly because markets expect higher policy rates. That flows straight into discount rates, so into software valuations.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: Which brings us to the software numbers.

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: Meritech's latest pulse shows the median public software company on about four point three times annual recurring revenue, down from four point five. Median net dollar retention has settled at a hundred and seven to a hundred and nine percent. And the line I'd underline is that companies growing faster at a similar Rule of Forty score trade at about seven point three times, against four point one for slower, more cash-generative peers. Growth is still what gets paid for.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: Confidence and scenarios?

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: High confidence. Base case, multiples stay compressed into twenty twenty-seven, and growth plus retention stay the levers that move valuation. Best case, AI volatility pushes investors toward mission-critical vertical software with durable retention, which is good company to be in. Worst case, a wobble in AI-linked credit tightens financing across the board, and private equity owners favour cash over growth investment. Watch the Fed on the ninth of December and the European Central Bank on the seventeenth.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: Quick pulse, then. Jordan?

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: Markets put about a ninety-six percent chance on a quarter-point Fed hike in December after a hotter-than-expected October core inflation reading from the personal consumption expenditures index. The dollar is just below its highs for the year. Sterling's around one dollar thirty-one, the euro about one dollar nine and a half cents.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: Europe?

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: Euro-area inflation is at four percent, double the target, so a December hike from the European Central Bank is widely expected. Brent crude is around ninety-two dollars a barrel, up from seventy-five in July.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: Right, three things to raise with the CFO. Jordan, go.

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: One. The build-out risk story is now public, so use it. British constraint costs were one point nine billion pounds last year and could reach seven point eight billion by twenty thirty, and this week's margin warnings tie grid reliability to how well capital work is sequenced. The ask is to tag UK pipeline opportunities where outage and delivery optimisation is a buying driver, and to fund some targeted marketing around the ED3 business plans in December.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: So it's not a new forecast, it's a better-labelled pipeline.

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: Exactly. Two. Resilience spend is rising, but so is affordability pressure. The WSSC example, a hundred and fifty-five million dollar need against a seven versus twelve percent rate fight, is the US pattern in miniature. The ask is to model a scenario where US water and municipal deals slip one or two quarters on budget pressure, alongside the upside where resilience mandates speed them up, and check the forecast isn't quietly assuming only the upside.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: And three?

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: Three. Benchmark the board story against what markets actually pay for, which is growth and net retention, with a public median of around a hundred and seven to a hundred and nine percent. And with a large asset management rival guiding to roughly flat growth, confirm deal desk guardrails in case competitors start bundling planning features into renewals.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: I'd sharpen that last one: decide the walk-away point before the first bundled offer turns up, not during the deal.

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: Couldn't have put it better myself. Well, I could, but not before coffee.

dialogue.speaker: ANCHOR
dialogue.text: That's the brief for Friday. Thanks to Priya and Sofia, and thanks to you for listening. Have a good weekend, and we'll be back on Monday.

dialogue.speaker: STRATEGIST
dialogue.text: Take care, everyone.
